fields.question: Why skip teacher correction for correct ME-OPD replies?
fields.answer: Successful traces retain task reward without stylistic interference. Failures alone select original tokens the teacher supports less. The teacher scores existing responses instead of writing new ones.
fields.example: Do not rewrite a valid alternative solution just because its style differs.

fields.question: How do ME-OPD and Projected Distillation produce corrections differently?
fields.answer: ME-OPD teacher-forces and suppresses chosen original error tokens. Projected Distillation generates a verified revision and compares edited spans via DPO. Scoring existing tokens and producing paired text differ.
fields.example: Only the latter needs a newly written answer aligned to the original.

fields.question: Compute ME-OPD group advantages before or after splitting successes and failures?
fields.answer: Use all K rewards before splitting. A success-only group has constant reward. Use frozen old student for strict-greater mask and divide by selected correction tokens across the minibatch.
fields.example: Teacher and old student ties are not selected; do not remake mask from updated scores.

fields.question: Why skip correction for successes and select only some tokens from failures?
fields.answer: Preserve successful student behavior with task reward. Compare teacher and old student only for errors, correcting less teacher-supported tokens. Full group advantage precedes split. Reference solution and full reply are teacher training inputs only.
fields.example: A misread geometry label can receive focused suppression without reworking a successful alternative response.

fields.question: Why align shared textual events rather than token IDs in CSD?
fields.answer: Tokenizers differ in IDs, vocabulary and segmentation. Verify decoded character spans, then compare probability of common text events.
fields.example: One tokenizer can split a word in two; identical IDs wouldn't establish matching text.

fields.question: What does REST preserve that renormalizing common candidates removes?
fields.answer: It retains probability of unmatched events instead of pretending their intersection is the whole distribution. Do not replace chain probability with a length mean.
fields.example: A small shared intersection may appear very similar after softmax while most mass was omitted.

fields.question: Do CSD student gradients flow only through the final token of a chunk?
fields.answer: No. Include prefix chain factors, final token and REST. Freeze teacher. Non-1:1 weights don't enter denominator count; fall back to CE for no KD/shared event and detach overall ratio.
fields.example: Ignoring the first of two pieces miscomputes its entire text event.

fields.question: Why preserve REST across tokenizers rather than softmax common matches?
fields.answer: Build common text events from verified decoded boundaries and chain probabilities. REST carries omitted mass; renormalization discards it and changes divergence. Don't align by position or IDs alone.
fields.example: Two tokens and one token may express one word, but unmatched continuation probability still exists.

fields.question: Why compare evidence-preserving and degraded crops in VAG?
fields.answer: Privileged corrections can mix visual evidence with style. Contrast matched visual conditions to estimate direction, retain agreeing corrections and bound modulation of verifier advantage.
fields.example: After cropping, check whether a teacher's revision follows changed visual evidence.

fields.question: How does VAG differ from fixed textual teacher logits?
fields.answer: The definition needs the same EMA vision model under real paired views. Fixed logits only simulate the formula, not visual sensitivity or attribution.
fields.example: Two manually supplied scores aren't an occlusion experiment.

fields.question: Can VAG's teacher branches be different models, and was this run?
fields.answer: Not under the same protocol: one EMA teacher, only visual input changes. The local page describes equations without executing multimodal training. Keep strict sign agreement and verifier advantage.
fields.example: Comparing a large vision teacher to a small text model confounds architecture and evidence.

fields.question: Why accept only teacher corrections matching the visual contrast sign?
fields.answer: Privileged crop changes may be stylistic. Require compatible evidence direction and use bounded modulation of verifier advantage. Only visual input changes in same EMA model; arbitrary text logits and local documentation do not reproduce the chain.
fields.example: If preference changes after privileged crop but not after occluding evidence, don't automatically treat it as visual guidance.

fields.question: Why interpolate APSD successes but extrapolate beyond teacher for failures?
fields.answer: Success should retain existing student preferences with gentle interpolation. Failures use stronger teacher-direction correction. Feedback selects a target regime, not guaranteed correctness.
fields.example: Use lighter changes after a correct response and stronger correction after failure.

fields.question: Why isn't freezing APSD self-teacher the same as detaching its entire target?
fields.answer: Teacher q is frozen, but product-of-experts target also depends differentiably on p. Whole-target detach removes a defining coupling term, despite identical forward values.
fields.example: Detaching a target branch partly built from current student changes optimization, not merely memory.

fields.question: Which PoE tensors retain APSD gradients, and how interpret default α?
fields.answer: Student and its target branch are differentiable, teacher detached. Use log space to avoid underflow. Correct α is between zero and one, error α above one. Local RLRF settings differ from paper RLVR.
fields.example: Local 0.5 and 1.5 aren't universal paper settings.

fields.question: Why freeze only APSD teacher rather than detach the interpolated/extrapolated target?
fields.answer: Target depends on current student as well as teacher. Detach loses the student coupling that differs for success/failure. Forward equality doesn't imply backward equality. Feedback is privileged training context only.
fields.example: Identical target probabilities can yield different parameter updates when only one graph retains target dependence.

fields.question: Is a SPOD decision one token or an action of multiple tokens?
fields.answer: Protect a full state-conditioned action including native termination, not one token or an episode. Labels are episode-level but protection is decision-specific.
fields.example: Tool name, arguments and terminator form one action within a possibly multi-action success.

fields.question: How does a SPOD soft floor differ from masking an entire successful episode?
fields.answer: Only selected actions are protected; other decisions still distill. A soft penalty below threshold isn't a hard guarantee and shared updates can change protected behavior.
fields.example: One useful successful decision need not block all teacher learning in its episode.

fields.question: Does SPOD compare temperature sampling probability or raw full-action probability?
fields.answer: Use raw pre-temperature/pre-constraint probabilities including termination, sum token logp. Recompute gate pre-update but detach it; average by action, state and episode so long traces don't dominate.
fields.example: Mean token probability isn't full-action probability and changes protection by length.

fields.question: Why protect full-action probabilities instead of token votes or masking the whole success?
fields.answer: A specific action in a success is protected when teacher supports it less; probability combines all its tokens. Cancel distillation there and add a soft floor, leaving other actions learnable. Shared parameter changes can still erode protected actions.
fields.example: Teacher can like some tool-call tokens and dislike others, so token votes can oppose the whole-call probability.

fields.question: Why organize TreeOPSD shared prefixes as a tree?
fields.answer: Different continuations from one history reveal outcomes. Back up leaf rewards with behavior likelihood into local credit and count shared turns once.
fields.example: Shared first three steps don't get duplicated because later branches differ.

fields.question: How does bounded Bernoulli teaching differ from repeatedly applying fixed advantage?
fields.answer: Frozen posterior gives a finite target: gradient stops at the desired relative change and reverses beyond it. Fixed advantages can keep pushing under repeated updates.
fields.example: After sufficient adjustment, stop rather than drive the action farther on the same batch.

fields.question: Is TreeOPSD's Bernoulli a full next-token teacher?
fields.answer: No. A two-point posterior describes a sampled turn relative to old policy. Use full actor-span likelihood and leaf-reward sample SD, exclude observations, and retain bounded-target derivation.
fields.example: The two outcomes are not two vocabulary tokens.

fields.question: Why convert backed-up tree credit into a bounded Bernoulli target?
fields.answer: Rewards set direction but no stopping distance. A fixed finite target stops or reverses gradients when reached or exceeded. Deduplicate shared turns and weight branches by full actor-span likelihood, not average token score.
fields.example: Repeatedly training one success group stops when it has learned enough instead of reinforcing indefinitely.
